title: All Together Now: The Collective Hero Stars in Who Moves America
author: Ed Rampell

**An Interview with Yael Bridge**

As socialism makes a comeback in public consciousness, _Who Moves America_
zooms in on union organizing and working class struggle. The 87-minute
documentary focuses on the 2023 showdown between the International Brotherhood
of Teamsters and United Parcel Service, as workers gear up for a possible
strike. The documentary is directed by Yael Bridge, who was Emmy-nominated for
producing 2017’s _Saving Capitalism_ , about former U.S. Labor Secretary
Robert Reich. In 2020, Bridge produced and directed _The Big Scary ‘S’ Word_ ,
about socialism.  _Who Moves America_ takes a close-up look at salt-of-the-
earth members of the Teamsters, that feisty, fabled union founded in 1903.
This was the last film to receive Corporation for Public Broadcasting funding
– which could explain why Trump put the CPB on the chopping block.
_CounterPunch_ interviewed Yael Bridge via Zoom in Portland, Oregon.

**What is _Who Moves America_ about?**

**Yael Bridge:** There’s a difference between theme and plot. The film is
really about solidarity and the democratic processes at its core.

_Who Moves America_ follows UPS Teamsters during the 2023 contract
negotiation. We follow a few different people in different parts of the
country, as well as the Teamsters’ president, Sean O’Brien in D.C., during the
negotiation process and lead up to when their contract would expire in what
was potentially one of the largest strikes in U.S. history. The UPS Teamsters’
contract is [for] the largest [private sector] bargaining unit in the country…
They’re one of the largest unions in America… the fifth largest… The people
that work there have a huge amount of leverage and power over our economic
system. So, it was obviously something we were very interested in exploring.

It is about how people work together and about things we can only do when we
do them together. That is what a union is. It’s just democracy in practice,
and the practice of building solidarity, which is not something that just
happens.

**What is the significance of UPS in the U.S. economy?**

UPS is the largest distribution company in the country. They’re far larger
than FedEx or DHL or USPS… It’s something like a third. I didn’t realize how
much bigger they were than everyone else when we started the film. 6% of GDP
goes through UPS every single day. They’re so powerful.

**Who owns United Parcel Service?**

It’s a publicly owned traded company. Shareholders own UPS… It’s a
corporation.

**How many people work for UPS?**

The bargaining unit for this contract was around 340,000 workers.

**Some people who work for UPS don’t belong to the Teamsters?**

There are plenty of people that work for UPS that are not unionized and are
not part of this contract.

**What industries do Teamsters** **work in?**

They are largely truck drivers, and in logistics. There’s Teamsters Hollywood;
they’re the stunt coordinators and the animal handlers. It’s not industry
specific; there’s lots of different people.

**In terms of the background of the Teamsters, for a period of time they had a
notorious history. Jimmy Hoffa was believed to be a very corrupt leader.**

Yeah. The Teamsters have a noted history, certainly, with Jimmy Hoffa. UPS was
always Teamsters. When UPS was founded, they were always unionized, which is
unique.

**How about the leadership now? Are they scandal-plagued?**

No, not at all. Sean O’Brien came in and the president right before him was
Jimmy Hoffa Jr. And Sean O’Brien campaigned very vigorously on winning. The
last contract they’d had in 2018 was full of concessions and it really was
considered a big step backwards. When Sean O’Brien campaigned, he campaigns
saying, “We’re going to be a fighting union again. We’re not going to work
past our contract expiration.” It was really very adamant about him going on
strike and standing firm. I think that that campaign rhetoric really inspired
not just his election winning, but really putting the wind behind his sails,
with all the workers feeling galvanized and enthusiastic about what was
possible. And then he was able to harness that to get a good contract in 2023.

**When O’Brien ran, was he part of a reform ticket?**

Without getting into too granular the Teamsters’ inner workings, he ran in
coalition with TDU, the Teamsters for a Democratic Union, which is the reform
caucus within the Teamsters.

**Your documentary essentially takes place in 2023, but there are lots of
flashbacks to 1997.**

1997 was the last time the Teamsters had gone on strike. It was a really big
strike and they won a lot of victories in that contract. So, it is this north
star that we found that a lot of workers are really talking about. “Can we go
back to our roots? Can we go back to this really big strike?” which helped the
people that worked there feel their power and agency. So, we were keen to
bring that element back in. It was one of the main throughlines because
organizing is cyclical, and you can win something and then it goes away after
all of these concessionary contracts. And you have to go out and fight for it
again. As people are aging, they’re not there anymore. You lose that history
and institutional knowledge of what that was like. And so, a lot of people
were feeling, “I was here in ’97, and this is my contract. I’m retiring and
these young people here don’t know what it’s like to go on strike. Don’t know
that type of solidarity.”

So much of being a Teamster is this concept of what comes after you’re gone.
They call them the unborn, the Teamsters-to-be. You don’t work at the
Teamsters yet but you will in five years. We are fighting so that you, future
Teamster, can have a good job and benefits and all these worker protections
and stuff. That’s something that gets reinforced when you do go on strike and
you see the benefits you’re fighting for play out over the decades. We really
want to hit hard that theme of intergenerational solidarity.

**What were the Teamsters’ top contract concerns and grievances in 2023?**

There were several main things they were really focusing on. A big one was a
two-tier pay structure they have for a category of worker called the “224,”
which was created in the 2018 contract negotiations. It’s sort of jargony, but
basically it just meant you got to keep your rate, but if you started working
after the 2018 contract, you were coming in as this different category of
worker that was created called 224, where you would get paid less. So, even
though your job would be virtually identical, to everyone that came before
you, you were paid substantially less. You had less protections. So, they
really, really wanted to get rid of that and bring everyone up that was a 224
to where they would have been had there not been that category of worker.

Another big one was air conditioning being put in the trucks. People are
literally dying in their trucks because they’re getting too hot. As we all
know, climate change is real and catastrophic and people are working in areas
where the temperatures are just increasing and increasing. Without air
conditioning in these trucks, it can get upwards of 140 degrees. So, it’s too
hot, and you’re outside all day, delivering packages, doing this really hard
physical labor, and there’s no air conditioning.

**With this two-tier system was there a discrepancy not only in wages but in
terms of the benefits that parttime and fulltime workers would get?**

That’s even different from the 224 category. The parttime and fulltime divide
at UPS… generally, if you’re a fulltime worker, you work in a truck and do
deliveries. And if you’re a parttime worker, then you work in the warehouse
doing sorting and packaging or pre-loading. Those are different categories of
workers with different benefits and wages. They’re both on the same contract,
even though the job description and benefits and wages are different. Another
thing they were trying to do with this contract was to bring those wages
closer together… so they would be in more collaboration and solidarity.

**Describe the Teamsters’ rank and file?**

Working at UPS as a Teamster is one of the few jobs that you can get without a
college degree and make six figures and get a pension. So, it is a really
important job in a lot of communities that otherwise aren’t able to make that
much money.

…What’s exciting about the Teamsters is that it is a really diverse
membership. It cuts across not just racial, age or gender but the political
divide, as well. Traditionally, Teamsters are more conservative, certainly
than maybe UAW, and are also an incredibly powerful fighting union. We were
really interested in exploring the nonpartisan nature of the work they were
doing without getting into the Republican/Democrat divide.

**Where did you shoot _Who Moves America_?**

We filmed largely in San Marcos, California, and in New York City and
Louisville, Kentucky.

**A lot of the workers there are Black and Hispanic.**

Yeah…

**What did the Teamsters’ union do to prepare for a potential strike during
the contract negotiation period?**

One thing they did to prepare for the strike was to go out on practice pickets
in front of the warehouses and facilities. That meant the workers would go set
up a picket line, and really get ready, and have their signs ready, and
generate press and really show the power they have to UPS. To be able to show
them: “Look, we can close this entrance.”

Those were not just educational for them, it also helped generate a lot of
really supportive buzz in the press. And it ended up being something that
helped turn the tables in those negotiations… This was definitely not a
contract negotiation that was last minute at all. They had been preparing for
it for years. You begin your contract fight as soon as you sign your current
contract, you start getting ready for the next contract. There’s certainly a
cyclical nature to this work. So, they’ve been preparing for a long time and
we’d been filming for a long time, as well.

**Let’s discuss some of the key individuals in your film, starting with the
most prominent person, General President of the International Brotherhood of
Teamsters, Sean O’Brien.**

Sean O’Brien is from Boston. He does come from a Teamsters family. Personally,
I heard him speak at Labor Notes before I’d even thought about filming with
him. I just thought he was a really dynamic speaker, he really motivated the
whole room.

**Tell us about some of the other organizers and union members in your film?**

We filmed with Antonio Rosario in New York and Antoine Andrews. They were
around in ’97 and have been involved in the union for a long time and also do
some work around organizing Amazon. Just were able to show us what it is like
to have a union job for so long, and how you’re able to provide for your
family and raise children and have a decent house with that kind of job.

We were filming in San Marcos with a bunch of guys who called themselves
“Strike Force” who were gearing up, preparing themselves for a long time for
this contract negotiation. They would meet very early in the morning before
their shift would start at a local deli and go over what was going on that
week in their job, and going out around the country. There were several people
in there we filmed with, and the one that’s most depicted in the film is
Justin [Alo]. He’s a father of two and was a 224 category worker. He’s just
sort of getting into the organizing efforts and seeing what it’s all about and
is this a good use of his time and energy and how to implement change.

In Kentucky, in Louisville, we were filming with two sisters, Angel [Badu] and
Nailah [Weller], who both worked for UPS. One of them was in college and one
of them had already graduated, and they were working parttime [at UPS] and
they had other parttime jobs, as well, at a McDonald’s and a Walgreens, I
think.

**Regarding the contract negotiations, what was the outcome?**

They got huge gains from this contract. Not only did they get raises for part-
timers and for full-timers and they got air conditioning being put in their
trucks. They had fans put in to retrofit some of their trucks. They also got
MLK Day as a national holiday. They got an ability to transport your job from
different locations.

**What percent of the UPS workers voted yes?**

I believe 80-something.

**Why were some UPS workers holdouts who didn’t sign the new contract or vote
“yes”?**

I’ve been hanging around a bunch of unions and union organizers for some time
now and filmed with several contract negotiations. There’s an interesting and
necessary thing that happens where you’re ramping up to what could be a
strike, or maybe is a strike. You’re a worker and you’re feeling your power
and it’s exciting, and you think you’re going to get all of these things. Then
ultimately, you get to a point, whether this is in a contract negotiation or a
strike, and you get a TA, your Tentative Agreement, this is what the
negotiating team and company have landed on. Then you have to decide as a
worker: Is this for you? Is this everything you want? Do you think you can get
more?

That is such a scary and personal situation. Because maybe for you, it is good
enough, but maybe for your neighbor it’s not. Maybe he needs something a lot
more. And, you can go on strike, and will you get everything – or will it go
horribly wrong? That’s just different people’s threshold for risk and reward.
For some people, this was an amazing contract and more than they could ever
hope for. For some people, it wasn’t good enough and they think they could
have gotten more.

Then there’s another category that says there’s value in going on strike, even
if you get what you would have gotten had you not gone on strike. There’s
value in going on strike in and of itself, because of all the work that you
do, and the connections and solidarity that is built, and putting fear into
the bosses… That power can’t be comparable to a comparable win in terms of
wages, there’s not a monetary value necessarily for that.

**Something that comes across in _Who Moves America_ is that the UPS workers
seem to have a sense of solidarity that transcends their union and they
realize that a victory for them is a triumph for the entire working class.
Tell us about that class consciousness?**

Certainly, the subtext for the whole movement we were documenting is Amazon,
and Amazon is just this giant, unorganized workforce. So much of what was
motivating Teamsters and the workers through this past contract negotiation
was trying to show force and flex their muscle for organizing Amazon workers.
There was so much solidarity around the people that work at Amazon. Also, as a
historical footnote, this was happening during a “Hot Labor Summer,” so there
were strikes happening all over the place. The Writers Guild and SAG were on
strike, Starbucks and Trader Joe’s workers were starting to organize around
then, there was a lot of labor fever. It felt like had the Teamsters gone on
strike this would have really pushed things a lot forward in that direction.

**Even though the UPS workers didn’t actually end up walking off the job, the
moral of your story seems best summed up by Frederick Douglass in 1857: “Power
concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will. Find out
just what any people will quietly submit to and you have found out the exact
measure of injustice and wrong which will be imposed upon them, and these will
continue till they are resisted with either words or blows, or with both. The
limits of tyrants are prescribed by the endurance of those whom they
oppress.”**

Yeah. People are really tired right now. It’s a really exhausting time to be
human… Reflective in that quote, is okay, I just submit, I can’t keep fighting
this. But that is losing, the concession. What these Teamsters showed is how
much they weren’t willing to do that anymore. One of the things that struck me
most about the Teamsters was that there was an offer that was just going to
raise the wages of the drivers. It was a disproportionate raise for the full-
timers and a very, very low wage for the part-timers. And the part-timers have
a huge amount of turnover, because the job is not very good and is very, very
hard… it’s grueling, very unpleasant. There isn’t necessarily incentive to
fight for the part-timers because they will literally be gone very likely.
Yet, they voted not to take that deal, to say no, we want to fight, even for
the part-timers. There’s a huge lesson for all of us: Even if you get a bit
for yourself, it really needs to be spread out among all of us. And if you
don’t do that, then it is just this slow walk towards death… you just keep
losing.

**Yael, the last full-length documentary you directed was 2020’s _The Big
Scary ‘S’ Word_ , about socialism. Is there a socialist faction inside the
Teamsters’ union?**

I think there’s a socialist faction everywhere… in every space. Whether
there’s socialist organizers within the Teamsters is not depicted in the film.

**Your film is being released while we seem to be having something of a
socialist moment. Democratic Socialists of America and other leftists are
winning and competing – well, maybe since they’re socialists, that’s the wrong
word, so let’s say “contending” – strongly in elections. Socialism is being
discussed – if not exactly intelligently debated – in what passes for
America’s public discourse. Your film is rooted not in intellectuals or
academics but in actual class struggle, your protagonists are blue collar
workers, real working class heroes. It’s not theory – it’s practice.**

They are working class heroes. [Laughs.] Thanks Ed, I feel seen… It is their
lives. I think they are heroic. It is also ordinary. What I am interested in
is not heroes, in the traditional sort of Marvel superhero and they fly or
whatever! You also see in documentary a lot – I think it’s a huge problem –
here’s a film about public schools, but it’s really about a single teacher and
how hard her job is and how she gives so much. You leave the film and you’re
moved – “She’s such a beautiful soul, she’s so generous.” That’s not unique to
her – that’s most teachers. And the film doesn’t talk about why it’s so hard
for her. As a viewer, it’s incredibly disempowering. You don’t know where to
put your emotions, your energy.

_Who Moves America_ has lots of heroes; it’s an ensemble cast. We didn’t want
to focus on just one person. It’s about how we’re able to work together and
collectively. Any one of those people in the film could go to their supervisor
and say, “I’m really hot. Could I get an air conditioner put in my truck?” And
we laugh because we know that would never happen… But if you get _everyone_
together and you all say, “We need air conditioners put in our trucks or we’re
not going to work anymore,” suddenly you’re all going to get air conditioners.

We can all be heroes. That’s not a magical thing someone is born with; that’s
something we need to find more examples of, which aren’t hard to find. They’re
everyday. We just don’t see them a lot in our movie screens and books. So, how
do we shift the stories we tell ourselves so we can see ourselves in them and
be the heroes we need to be?

**_Who Moves America_ is executive produced by Steven Bognar, who exec
produced and co-directed 2020’s Best Documentary Oscar winner _American
Factory_ , co-made with Julia Reichert. The day before Reichert quoted Marx in
her Academy Award acceptance speech, at the Spirit Awards I asked Reichert –
who’d previously been Oscar-nominated for the 1976 and 1983 documentaries
Union Maids and Seeing Red, which was about Communist Party USA members – if
she thought “socialism is the answer to income inequality?” **

**Reichert replied: “Do I think socialism is the answer for our country? We
should all. . . share the wealth. We should tax rich people more than they
are. Healthcare should be for all. It’s more like what I would call
‘democratic socialism feminism.’”**

**Yael, how would you answer that question? Would a form of socialism solve
the problems of Teamsters and other proletarians?**

We have an extremely unequal distribution of resources. That is indisputable
and unconscionable. I don’t understand – I’m always looking for ways to
address that and level the playing field. Unions are one of the many levers we
have for flattening this just insanely unequal access to resources that people
have. The dangers of these unequal resources aren’t just that they’re unfair
or it means I might die sooner because I don’t have health insurance… It’s
impossible to have democracy and such unequal access to resources…

**How do you define socialism?**

I am on the board of the DSA Fund. There are many ways we can get to a more
equitable and democratic world. One of those is at the ballot box, and we see
that with more Democratic Socialists campaigning and winning and then doing an
incredible job in office, and that gives me lots of hope. And another of the
levers we have is labor unions, and that’s what I was focusing on in this
film.

**We’ve covered a lot of ground. Is there anything you’d like to add?**

Another of our executive producers is [author/filmmaker] Astra Taylor. The
team is so strong. Everyone on the team has a background in making labor
films. It’s a collaborative effort.

**What are some of your favorite labor films?**

…I love everything Boots Riley does…. _I Love Boosters_ feels like a really
good companion piece to our film, it ends where our film picks up. I really
love _Union_ that Stephen Maing and Brett Story directed about organizing the
Amazon Labor Union with Chris Smalls. One of their producers, Mars Verrone,
produced our film as well.

_Who Moves America_ is being screened 5:00 p.m., Sept. 5 at the Socialism
Conference in Chicago and theatrically opens Sept. 9 (the exact 50th
anniversary of Chairman Mao’s death), including some Q&As at screenings with
Yael Bridge. See: <https://www.whomovesamerica.com/screenings>.
